description: Devices requesting an IP address receive no response at all from the DHCP server, leaving them without network configuration.
symptoms: Devices fail to get an IP and fall back to an APIPA (169.254.x.x) address
ipconfig /renew hangs or times out
Multiple new devices joining the network are all affected
possible_causes: DHCP service on the router or server has crashed or stopped
DHCP server is unreachable due to a network path problem
DHCP relay agent misconfigured on a multi-subnet network
Router/server overloaded or out of resources
diagnostic_questions: Is this affecting one device or all new devices joining the network?
Is the DHCP server a router, or a dedicated server (Windows Server, Linux, etc.)?
Has anything changed recently, like a router replacement or firmware update?
Can you reach the DHCP server's management interface at all?

commands.purpose: Attempt to get a response from the DHCP server
commands.expected_result: A valid IP address is returned
commands.abnormal_result: Request times out or fails, confirming no response from the DHCP server

commands.purpose: Check if the DHCP server itself is reachable on the network
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout suggests the server is down or unreachable, not just its DHCP service

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm whether multiple devices are affected, indicating a server-wide problem rather than one device
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Narrows the scope of troubleshooting significantly

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if the DHCP server (router or dedicated server) is powered on and reachable via ping
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out a complete outage of the device hosting DHCP

troubleshooting_steps.action: On a router, log into its admin page and confirm the DHCP server feature is enabled
troubleshooting_steps.reason: DHCP can sometimes be accidentally disabled during other configuration changes

troubleshooting_steps.action: On a dedicated DHCP server, check that the DHCP service is running (services.msc on Windows, or systemctl status isc-dhcp-server on Linux)
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the service itself has stopped

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the DHCP service or the device hosting it
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves most temporary crashes or hangs

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for a full DHCP scope (address pool) if the service is running but still not responding to new requests
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A depleted address pool can cause the server to effectively stop answering new clients

possible_solutions: Restart the DHCP service or the router/server hosting it
Confirm DHCP is enabled in router/server settings
Increase the DHCP scope size if depleted
Check network path to the DHCP server for connectivity issues
prevention: Monitor DHCP service uptime on critical infrastructure
Keep router/server firmware and OS updated
Set up alerts for DHCP scope utilization nearing capacity

description: The DHCP process fails outright on a client device, shown as an explicit 'DHCP failed' or similar error rather than a silent timeout.
symptoms: Explicit error such as 'DHCP is not enabled for this adapter' or 'DHCP failed'
Adapter shows no valid IP configuration
Error appears in Windows Event Viewer network diagnostics
possible_causes: DHCP disabled on the network adapter itself (manually set to static previously without full configuration)
Corrupted TCP/IP stack on the client
DHCP Client service stopped on the computer
Group Policy or software disabling automatic IP configuration
diagnostic_questions: Is the adapter set to obtain an IP address automatically, or is it manually configured?
Is the DHCP Client Windows service running?
Does this happen on this device only, or across the network?
Has any recent software or policy change affected network settings?

commands.purpose: Check whether the adapter is configured for DHCP or has a static configuration
commands.expected_result: Shows 'DHCP Enabled: Yes' with a valid assigned address
commands.abnormal_result: Shows 'DHCP Enabled: No', confirming the adapter is set to static rather than automatic

commands.purpose: Check whether the DHCP Client service is running on this computer
commands.expected_result: Service status is 'Running'
commands.abnormal_result: Service is stopped, which will prevent DHCP configuration entirely

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the adapter's IP settings to confirm 'Obtain an IP address automatically' is selected
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A manually configured static IP will show DHCP as disabled, which is expected behavior in that case, not a fault

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the DHCP Client service is running in Windows Services
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This core service is required for any DHCP-based configuration to succeed

troubleshooting_steps.action: Start the DHCP Client service if stopped and set it to automatic
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the issue if this specific service was the cause

troubleshooting_steps.action: Run netsh int ip reset to reset the TCP/IP stack if the adapter still fails after confirming DHCP is enabled and the service is running
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves deeper corruption preventing DHCP negotiation

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check Group Policy settings on managed/work computers for any restriction on automatic IP configuration
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Administrators sometimes intentionally enforce static IPs via policy

possible_solutions: Set the adapter to obtain an IP address automatically
Start and enable the DHCP Client service
Reset the TCP/IP stack with netsh int ip reset
Check Group Policy for IP configuration restrictions on managed devices
prevention: Avoid manually disabling the DHCP Client service
Keep TCP/IP stack healthy with periodic system maintenance
Document any intentional static IP policies for managed devices

description: From the network administrator's perspective, one or more clients cannot obtain an IP address, and the cause needs to be found on the DHCP server side rather than the client.
symptoms: Multiple clients report no internet or an APIPA address
DHCP server logs show failed or declined requests
New devices in particular are affected more than existing ones
possible_causes: DHCP scope (address pool) is full
DHCP server has a misconfigured scope, such as a wrong range or exclusions
DHCP relay agent not forwarding requests correctly across VLANs/subnets
Rogue or unauthorized DHCP server on the network interfering
diagnostic_questions: How many clients are affected, and are they all on the same subnet or VLAN?
Is the DHCP scope size sufficient for the number of devices on the network?
Is there any possibility of a second, unauthorized DHCP server on the network?
Are affected clients on a different subnet from the DHCP server, requiring a relay agent?

commands.purpose: Confirm the client's current failed state to correlate with server-side logs
commands.expected_result: Shows the DHCP server address the client attempted to contact
commands.abnormal_result: No DHCP server address recorded at all, suggesting the request never reached any server

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the DHCP server's scope statistics for current utilization versus total pool size
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A nearly or fully exhausted scope is one of the most common administrative causes

troubleshooting_steps.action: Review the DHCP server logs for declined or failed lease requests and their reasons
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides specific technical detail on why requests are failing

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for the presence of a second, unauthorized DHCP server using a tool or by reviewing switch port/device inventory
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A rogue DHCP server can hand out conflicting or invalid configurations, causing seemingly random failures

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify DHCP relay agent configuration on routers/switches if affected clients are on a different subnet than the DHCP server
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Without proper relay configuration, DHCP broadcasts never reach a server on another subnet

troubleshooting_steps.action: Expand the DHCP scope or adjust exclusions if the pool is genuinely undersized for the network
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides enough addresses for all current and near-future devices

possible_solutions: Expand the DHCP scope size
Correct DHCP relay agent configuration for multi-subnet networks
Locate and disable any unauthorized/rogue DHCP server
Review and correct scope exclusions or reservations causing address shortages
prevention: Regularly monitor DHCP scope utilization
Restrict who can connect unauthorized routers/servers to the network
Document DHCP relay configuration for all subnets/VLANs
keywords: dhcp scope full clients cant connect

description: The DHCP server's pool of available IP addresses has been completely used up, so no new devices can receive an address.
symptoms: New devices cannot get an IP address, while existing connected devices continue to work fine
DHCP server admin console shows scope utilization at or near 100%
Error logs show 'No addresses available' or similar
possible_causes: More devices connected to the network than the scope was originally sized for
Old, disconnected devices still holding leases that have not expired
Scope range configured too small for the network's needs
Excessive DHCP reservations reducing the available dynamic pool
diagnostic_questions: How many devices are typically connected, versus the total size of the DHCP scope?
Have many new devices, like phones or IoT devices, been added recently?
What is the current DHCP lease time, and could expired but unreleased leases be a factor?
Are there many static reservations reducing the usable dynamic range?

commands.purpose: View DHCP scope details and utilization on a Windows DHCP server
commands.expected_result: Shows the scope range and number of addresses in use versus available
commands.abnormal_result: Available addresses at or near zero, confirming the scope is full

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the current DHCP scope utilization statistics on the server or router
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms the scope is genuinely full rather than another DHCP problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Review and remove old, stale, or duplicate leases for devices no longer on the network
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Frees up addresses that are being unnecessarily held

troubleshooting_steps.action: Expand the DHCP scope range if the network's device count has grown beyond the original sizing
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly increases the number of available addresses for new devices

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reduce the DHCP lease time if addresses are being held longer than necessary by inactive devices
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Shorter leases free up unused addresses more quickly for reassignment

troubleshooting_steps.action: Review static reservations and exclusions to ensure they are not unnecessarily reducing the dynamic pool
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Reservations should only be used for devices that genuinely need a fixed address

possible_solutions: Expand the DHCP scope range
Clear stale or expired leases manually
Reduce the DHCP lease time to free addresses faster
Review and minimize unnecessary static reservations/exclusions
prevention: Size DHCP scopes with future growth in mind
Periodically audit and clean up old leases and reservations
Monitor scope utilization trends over time to anticipate exhaustion

description: From an administrative view, many client leases are expiring around the same time and failing to renew properly, causing widespread but temporary connectivity loss.
symptoms: Multiple devices lose connectivity around the same time of day
DHCP server logs show many leases expiring in a short window
Devices recover on their own or after a manual renew/reconnect
possible_causes: DHCP lease time configured too short for the environment's usage pattern
DHCP server was briefly unavailable during a mass renewal window
Network outage coincided with a renewal window, causing widespread failures
Server resource exhaustion when handling many simultaneous renewal requests
diagnostic_questions: What is the currently configured DHCP lease time?
Do the affected devices' leases appear to have started/renewed around the same time originally, causing them to expire in a batch?
Was the DHCP server or network down at all during the affected time window?
Does this happen predictably, such as every morning when devices wake up together?

commands.purpose: Review lease times and current lease statistics for the scope
commands.expected_result: Lease times and renewal patterns appear reasonable and staggered
commands.abnormal_result: A large cluster of leases expiring at the same time, suggesting a synchronized renewal problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Review DHCP server logs for the time window when multiple devices lost connectivity
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether this is indeed a mass lease expiration event rather than unrelated individual issues

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if the DHCP server experienced any downtime or resource strain during that window
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A server that was briefly unavailable during a renewal spike would explain the widespread failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Review the configured DHCP lease time and consider adjusting it to better suit the environment, such as longer leases for stable networks
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An appropriately sized lease time reduces the frequency and clustering of renewal events

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ensure the DHCP server has adequate resources (CPU, memory, network capacity) to handle simultaneous renewal bursts
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Prevents server overload from causing a cascading mass failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Monitor for recurrence at the same time of day and correlate with any other scheduled network events, such as backups or maintenance windows
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Identifies if another process is interfering with the DHCP server during that time

possible_solutions: Adjust DHCP lease time to reduce clustering of renewal events
Ensure the DHCP server has sufficient resources for peak renewal load
Investigate and resolve any recurring server downtime during renewal windows
Stagger device connection patterns where feasible
prevention: Choose lease times appropriate for the network's stability and device count
Monitor DHCP server performance and resource usage
Schedule maintenance windows to avoid peak renewal times
keywords: many devices lose connection same time

description: The DHCP server software or service has stopped running entirely, whether on a router or a dedicated server, halting all new address assignments network-wide.
symptoms: No new devices can obtain an IP address anywhere on the network
DHCP service explicitly shows as 'Stopped' in service management tools
Existing devices with unexpired leases may continue working temporarily
possible_causes: Service crashed due to a software bug or resource exhaustion
Service was manually or accidentally stopped by an administrator
Dependent service (like a database backend for enterprise DHCP) failed
Server or router experienced a reboot and the service did not auto-start
diagnostic_questions: Is this a router-based or dedicated server-based DHCP service?
Was any recent maintenance, update, or configuration change performed?
Does the DHCP service show as stopped, or is it running but unresponsive?
Are existing connected devices still working, suggesting only new leases are affected?

commands.purpose: Check DHCP service status on a Linux-based DHCP server
commands.expected_result: Shows 'active (running)'
commands.abnormal_result: Shows 'inactive (dead)' or 'failed', confirming the service is stopped

commands.command: services.msc (DHCP Server service, on Windows Server)
commands.purpose: Check DHCP service status on a Windows Server DHCP role
commands.expected_result: Status is 'Running'
commands.abnormal_result: Status is 'Stopped', confirming the service needs to be restarted

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the DHCP service status using the appropriate command or tool for the platform (Windows Services or systemctl on Linux)
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms definitively whether the service is stopped versus another underlying issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Attempt to start the DHCP service
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the immediate outage if the service simply stopped

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check system/service logs for the reason the service stopped, such as a crash or resource error
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Identifies the root cause to prevent recurrence

troubleshooting_steps.action: Set the DHCP service to start automatically on boot if it is not already configured that way
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Prevents the service from staying down after a server or router reboot

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for and resolve any underlying resource issues (disk space, memory) on the server if the service crashed due to resource exhaustion
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Addresses the root cause rather than just restarting the symptom

possible_solutions: Start the DHCP service
Set the service to start automatically on boot
Investigate and resolve logged errors causing the crash
Free up server resources if exhaustion caused the crash
prevention: Set critical services to automatic startup
Monitor DHCP service uptime with alerting
Perform regular maintenance and resource monitoring on DHCP servers

description: The DHCP server is running and assigning addresses, but the configuration values it hands out (gateway, DNS, subnet, etc.) are wrong, causing widespread connectivity issues for clients.
symptoms: All or most clients on the network have connectivity problems despite receiving an IP address
Clients report wrong gateway, DNS, or subnet values in their configuration
Problem appeared after a change to the DHCP server's scope options
possible_causes: Wrong default gateway configured in the DHCP scope options
Wrong DNS server addresses configured in the scope options
Incorrect subnet mask or address range configured in the scope
Scope options recently changed incorrectly during maintenance
diagnostic_questions: What scope options are currently configured on the DHCP server, especially gateway and DNS?
Did anyone recently change the DHCP server or scope configuration?
Are all affected clients receiving the same incorrect values?
What are the correct values that should be configured?

commands.purpose: See exactly what configuration values the client received from DHCP
commands.expected_result: Correct gateway, DNS, and subnet values matching the real network
commands.abnormal_result: Incorrect values matching a misconfigured scope, confirming the server-side configuration is at fault

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check an affected client's received configuration with ipconfig /all to see the exact incorrect values
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms precisely what is wrong and needs correcting on the server

troubleshooting_steps.action: Log into the DHCP server or router admin interface and review the scope options for gateway, DNS, and subnet
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Identifies the specific misconfigured setting

troubleshooting_steps.action: Correct the scope options to match the actual, correct network values
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly fixes what all future DHCP clients will receive

troubleshooting_steps.action: Have affected clients release and renew their IP address to pick up the corrected configuration
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Existing clients will not get the corrected settings until their next renewal

troubleshooting_steps.action: Document the corrected configuration to prevent the same mistake in future changes
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Reduces the risk of this recurring during future maintenance

possible_solutions: Correct the DHCP scope options (gateway, DNS, subnet) to the proper values
Have clients release and renew to receive the corrected configuration
Document the correct configuration for future reference
prevention: Test DHCP scope changes on a single device before wide rollout
Maintain clear documentation of intended DHCP scope settings
Use change control processes for DHCP server modifications

description: A device that should receive a specific reserved (fixed) IP address through a DHCP reservation instead receives a different, dynamic address.
symptoms: Device with a known DHCP reservation gets a different IP address than expected
Reservation appears configured correctly in the DHCP server settings
May cause issues for services expecting the device at its reserved address, like port forwarding or a printer setup
possible_causes: Reservation configured with an incorrect MAC address
Device's actual MAC address changed, such as after a network card replacement or virtual machine reconfiguration
Reservation address falls outside the active DHCP scope range
DHCP server has not yet applied or synchronized the reservation
diagnostic_questions: What MAC address is configured in the reservation, and does it match the device's actual current MAC address?
Is the reserved IP address within the DHCP server's active scope range?
Has the device's network hardware been replaced or reconfigured recently, such as a new network card or VM network adapter?
Has the device been rebooted or had its IP released and renewed since the reservation was created?

commands.purpose: Check the device's actual current MAC address and assigned IP
commands.expected_result: MAC address matches what is configured in the DHCP reservation
commands.abnormal_result: MAC address differs from the reservation, explaining why the reserved IP was not assigned

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the device's actual current MAC address using ipconfig /all
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides the ground truth to compare against the reservation's configured MAC address

troubleshooting_steps.action: Compare this to the MAC address entered in the DHCP server's reservation settings
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A mismatch is the most common cause of a reservation not being honored

troubleshooting_steps.action: Correct the MAC address in the reservation if it does not match
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ensures the DHCP server can correctly identify this specific device for the reservation

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the reserved IP address falls within the DHCP server's active scope range
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A reservation outside the active range will not be properly applied

troubleshooting_steps.action: Release and renew the IP address on the device after correcting the reservation
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Forces the device to request a new address, which should now honor the corrected reservation

possible_solutions: Correct the MAC address in the DHCP reservation
Ensure the reserved IP falls within the active DHCP scope
Release and renew the device's IP address after correcting the reservation
prevention: Document reservations with device names and MAC addresses clearly
Update reservations promptly after hardware changes
Periodically audit reservations against actual connected devices

description: The configured DNS server does not respond to lookup requests, so domain names cannot be translated into IP addresses even though the network connection itself works.
symptoms: Browser shows 'DNS server not responding' or similar error
Websites fail to load by name, but pinging a raw IP address works fine
Problem may affect one or all devices on the network
possible_causes: DNS server (often the router or ISP's DNS) is down or unreachable
Network connectivity issue preventing DNS queries from reaching the server
Firewall blocking DNS traffic (port 53)
Misconfigured DNS server address on the device
diagnostic_questions: Does pinging a known IP address like 8.8.8.8 work, even though website names do not load?
Are you using the router's default DNS, or a custom DNS server like Google or Cloudflare?
Does this affect all devices on the network or just one?
Has the DNS server address configuration changed recently?

commands.purpose: Directly query the configured DNS server for a domain lookup
commands.expected_result: Returns a valid IP address for the domain
commands.abnormal_result: 'DNS request timed out' or 'No response from server' confirms the DNS server is not responding

commands.purpose: Confirm general internet connectivity is fine, isolating the problem to DNS specifically
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout would indicate a broader connectivity problem, not just DNS

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ping a known public IP address to confirm general internet connectivity works
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether this is truly a DNS-specific problem or a broader connectivity issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Run nslookup on a well-known domain to directly test the configured DNS server
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms the DNS server itself is not responding to queries

troubleshooting_steps.action: Switch the DNS server setting to a reliable public DNS like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Bypasses a malfunctioning or unreachable DNS server

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the router if it also acts as the local DNS server/forwarder
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves a temporary crash or hang in the router's DNS service

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check firewall settings for any rule blocking DNS traffic on port 53
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A firewall blocking this specific port would prevent all DNS queries from succeeding

possible_solutions: Switch to a reliable public DNS server like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1
Restart the router if it handles local DNS
Check and correct firewall rules blocking port 53
Contact the ISP if their DNS servers are confirmed down
prevention: Configure a reliable secondary DNS server as a backup
Keep router firmware updated for DNS service stability
Periodically verify DNS server responsiveness on critical systems

description: A specific domain name, or all domain names, cannot be translated into an IP address, resulting in failed website loads despite a working internet connection.
symptoms: Browser error such as 'DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN' or 'Server not found'
Pinging the domain name fails, but pinging its IP address directly (if known) works
May affect one domain or all domains depending on the cause
possible_causes: DNS server has no record or an outdated record for the domain
Domain itself may have DNS configuration issues (if it's a custom/internal domain)
Local DNS cache holding a bad or outdated entry
Typo in the domain name being entered
diagnostic_questions: Is this happening with one specific domain or website names in general?
Have you tried a different DNS server to see if resolution works there instead?
Is this a public website or an internal company domain?
Have you double-checked the domain name is spelled correctly?

commands.purpose: Directly test resolution of the specific domain in question
commands.expected_result: Returns a valid IP address for the domain
commands.abnormal_result: 'Non-existent domain' or no answer confirms a resolution failure for this specific name

commands.purpose: Clear the local DNS resolver cache of any outdated entries
commands.expected_result: Cache successfully flushed
commands.abnormal_result: N/A - this is a corrective action, not a diagnostic result

troubleshooting_steps.action: Double-check the domain name is typed correctly, without typos
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A simple typo is a surprisingly common cause of resolution failures

troubleshooting_steps.action: Run nslookup directly against the domain to see the exact DNS response
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether this is a genuine DNS resolution failure and what the server is actually returning

troubleshooting_steps.action: Flush the local DNS cache with ipconfig /flushdns
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Clears any stale or corrupted cached entry for this domain

troubleshooting_steps.action: Try resolving the domain using a different DNS server, such as 8.8.8.8
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines if the issue is specific to the currently configured DNS server

troubleshooting_steps.action: For internal/custom domains, check with the domain administrator whether the DNS record exists and is correctly configured
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Internal domains depend on proper internal DNS zone configuration, which may need admin correction

possible_solutions: Flush the DNS cache
Try a different DNS server
Verify the domain name is spelled correctly
Contact the domain's DNS administrator for internal/custom domains
prevention: Keep DNS records properly maintained and documented for internal domains
Periodically flush DNS cache as routine maintenance
Double-check domain spelling before troubleshooting further

description: A general DNS lookup failure occurs, often shown as a generic error during nslookup or in application logs, without loading any website.
symptoms: nslookup or dig commands return timeout or failure errors
Applications relying on DNS fail to connect to their servers
Error may mention 'DNS lookup failed' or 'Could not resolve host'
possible_causes: DNS server unreachable or not responding
Local network adapter DNS settings misconfigured
Firewall or security software blocking DNS queries
Corrupted DNS resolver cache or Windows DNS Client service issue
diagnostic_questions: What specific error message appears during the failed lookup?
Are you able to reach the DNS server via ping, if its IP is known?
Does this affect all lookups or specific domains only?
Has this device's DNS configuration been checked recently?

commands.purpose: Perform a basic DNS lookup test to observe the exact failure
commands.expected_result: Returns a valid IP address
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout or error message provides detail on the specific type of DNS failure

commands.purpose: Check what DNS server addresses are currently configured
commands.expected_result: Valid, reachable DNS server addresses listed
commands.abnormal_result: Missing, blank, or incorrect DNS server entries explain the lookup failures

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the currently configured DNS server addresses with ipconfig /all
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the device even has valid DNS servers configured to query

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test connectivity to the configured DNS server with ping
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines if the DNS server itself is reachable on the network

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the DNS Client service in Windows Services (or the equivalent resolver service on other operating systems)
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves a stuck or corrupted local DNS resolver service

troubleshooting_steps.action: Switch to a known reliable public DNS server temporarily to test if the issue is server-specific
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the problem lies with the specific configured DNS server or something more local

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check firewall or security software for rules blocking DNS traffic (UDP/TCP port 53)
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Security software occasionally blocks DNS queries, especially after a recent update or policy change

possible_solutions: Restart the DNS Client/resolver service
Switch to a different, reliable DNS server
Adjust firewall rules blocking DNS traffic
Correct DNS server configuration on the adapter
prevention: Keep DNS resolver services running and set to automatic startup
Regularly verify DNS configuration on critical systems
Review firewall rules after updates for unintended DNS blocking

description: The device is configured to use a DNS server that is wrong, outdated, or no longer appropriate, causing resolution failures or unexpected results.
symptoms: Websites fail to load, load slowly, or resolve to unexpected addresses
DNS server address in network settings does not match what is expected
May cause security or filtering inconsistencies if using an unintended DNS server
possible_causes: Manually configured DNS server address is outdated or incorrect
VPN or other software silently changed the DNS server setting
ISP or router's default DNS server was changed without updating documentation
Leftover DNS configuration from a previous network environment
diagnostic_questions: What DNS server address is currently configured on this device?
Should this device be using automatic (router-provided) DNS, or a specific manually configured one?
Has any VPN or security software been installed recently that might change DNS settings?
Was this device recently moved from a different network without updating its DNS configuration?

commands.purpose: Check the currently configured DNS server addresses
commands.expected_result: DNS servers match the intended, correct configuration for this network
commands.abnormal_result: Unexpected, outdated, or incorrect DNS server addresses listed

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the currently configured DNS server addresses using ipconfig /all
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes exactly what is currently set, which may differ from what is assumed

troubleshooting_steps.action: Determine what the correct DNS server should be, whether automatic from the router or a specific manual choice
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides the target configuration to fix towards

troubleshooting_steps.action: Update the DNS server setting to the correct value, or set it to obtain DNS automatically
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the misconfiguration

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for VPN or security software that may be overriding DNS settings, and adjust its configuration if needed
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some software silently redirects DNS traffic, which can look like a manual misconfiguration

troubleshooting_steps.action: Flush the DNS cache after making changes to ensure old cached results do not linger
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Prevents confusion from stale results cached under the old DNS configuration

possible_solutions: Correct the DNS server address to the intended value
Set the adapter to obtain DNS automatically if manual configuration is not needed
Check VPN/security software for DNS override settings
Flush the DNS cache after changes
prevention: Document intended DNS configuration for company devices
Regularly audit DNS settings on critical systems
Review VPN/security software DNS behavior before deployment

description: Websites eventually load, but there is a noticeable delay specifically during the domain name lookup phase before the page begins loading.
symptoms: Noticeable pause before a webpage starts loading, especially on first visit to a site
Subsequent visits to the same site may load faster due to caching
Ping to the domain shows a delay before resolving, though the ping itself may be fast once resolved
possible_causes: Slow or overloaded DNS server
Geographically distant DNS server increasing round-trip time
ISP's DNS infrastructure experiencing performance issues
DNS server configured with multiple hops or forwarding chains adding delay
diagnostic_questions: Does the delay happen on every website, or mainly on first visits to new sites?
What DNS server is currently being used, the router's default, the ISP's, or a public one?
Have you tried switching to a different public DNS server to compare speed?
Does the delay happen consistently, or only at certain times of day?

commands.purpose: Manually time how long a DNS lookup takes using the current DNS server
commands.expected_result: Fast response, typically well under a second
commands.abnormal_result: Noticeably slow response confirms the DNS server itself is responding slowly

troubleshooting_steps.action: Time DNS lookups using nslookup against the current DNS server for a few different domains
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes a baseline of how slow the current resolution really is

troubleshooting_steps.action: Switch to a fast, well-known public DNS server like 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) or 8.8.8.8 (Google) and re-test
troubleshooting_steps.reason: These providers are generally optimized for low-latency responses and serve as a good comparison

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if the current DNS server is geographically distant or part of a slow ISP infrastructure
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Physical distance and server load both directly affect DNS response time

troubleshooting_steps.action: Consider using a DNS provider with built-in caching and performance optimization if the ISP's DNS remains slow
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides consistently faster resolution going forward

troubleshooting_steps.action: Clear the DNS cache and monitor if performance improves over time as new fast entries are cached
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A cache full of stale or slow-to-verify entries can also contribute to perceived slowness

possible_solutions: Switch to a faster public DNS server like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8
Flush the DNS cache
Choose a DNS provider with good performance and low latency for your region
prevention: Regularly benchmark DNS performance if speed is a priority
Use reputable, well-provisioned DNS providers
Keep router firmware updated if it handles local DNS forwarding

description: A company's internal DNS server, used for resolving internal resource names like file servers or intranet sites, is not resolving those names correctly for users.
symptoms: Internal resources like \\fileserver or intranet.company.local fail to resolve
External/public websites may still work fine, showing the problem is isolated to internal DNS
May affect all users or just those on certain subnets/VLANs
possible_causes: Internal DNS server (often a domain controller) service stopped or crashed
DNS zone records missing, incorrect, or not replicated
Client pointed to the wrong DNS server, such as a public DNS instead of the internal one
Internal DNS server unreachable due to network segmentation issues
diagnostic_questions: Are external/public websites still working, isolating this to internal name resolution?
What DNS server address are affected clients configured to use?
Is the internal DNS server (such as a domain controller) currently running and reachable?
Does this affect all users, or only certain subnets, VLANs, or office locations?

commands.purpose: Directly query the internal DNS server for an internal resource name
commands.expected_result: Returns the correct internal IP address for the resource
commands.abnormal_result: No response or an error indicates a problem with the internal DNS server or its records

commands.purpose: Confirm the internal DNS server itself is reachable on the network
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout suggests the internal DNS server is down or a network path issue exists

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm external websites still resolve normally to isolate the issue to internal DNS specifically
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Narrows the problem scope and rules out a general DNS or connectivity failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check that affected clients are pointed to the correct internal DNS server address
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Clients accidentally using a public DNS server will never resolve internal-only names

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the internal DNS server (often a domain controller) is powered on and its DNS service is running
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A stopped service or offline server explains a total internal resolution failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the relevant DNS zone for missing or incorrect records for the affected resource
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether this is a specific record issue rather than a server-wide outage

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check network connectivity and any relevant VLAN/subnet routing between affected clients and the internal DNS server
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Segmented networks require proper routing for clients to reach the internal DNS server at all

possible_solutions: Point affected clients to the correct internal DNS server
Restart the internal DNS service if stopped
Correct or recreate missing/incorrect DNS zone records
Fix network routing between affected subnets and the DNS server
prevention: Use DHCP to consistently distribute the correct internal DNS server to all clients
Regularly back up and audit internal DNS zone records
Monitor internal DNS server health and service uptime

description: A publicly used DNS server, such as Google's 8.8.8.8 or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, appears to not be working from the current network, even though it usually works fine.
symptoms: Manually configured public DNS server fails to resolve any domains
Switching back to the router's default DNS resolves the issue
May coincide with certain firewall or network configurations blocking external DNS
possible_causes: ISP or router blocking outbound DNS traffic to servers other than their own
Firewall rule blocking specific public DNS server IP addresses or DNS ports
Temporary outage or issue with the specific public DNS provider (rare but possible)
Router's DNS settings overriding client-configured DNS servers
diagnostic_questions: Does switching back to the router's automatic/default DNS resolve the issue?
Is there any firewall, parental control, or ISP-level restriction that might block third-party DNS servers?
Have you tried a different public DNS provider to see if the problem is specific to just one?
Is this a public network, like at a school, hotel, or workplace, that might intentionally restrict DNS choices?

commands.purpose: Directly test if the public DNS server responds when explicitly queried
commands.expected_result: Returns a valid response
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout or no response suggests the network is blocking traffic to this specific DNS server

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the public DNS server directly using nslookup with its address explicitly specified
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the server itself is reachable and responding from this specific network

troubleshooting_steps.action: Try switching back to the router's default/automatic DNS server to confirm normal DNS resolution otherwise works
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes that the problem is specific to using an alternate public DNS server, not general connectivity

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if this is a public, restricted, or managed network (school, workplace, hotel) that may intentionally block third-party DNS servers
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some networks deliberately force all DNS traffic through their own servers for content filtering or security

troubleshooting_steps.action: Try a different public DNS provider, such as switching from Google's 8.8.8.8 to Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps determine if the block is specific to one provider's servers or DNS traffic to outside servers in general

troubleshooting_steps.action: Use the network's provided/default DNS server if third-party DNS is confirmed to be blocked and cannot be changed
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Restores working DNS resolution within the network's restrictions

possible_solutions: Revert to the router's default/automatic DNS server if third-party DNS is blocked
Try a different public DNS provider
Contact the network administrator if a specific public DNS server needs to be allowed
prevention: Understand network DNS policies before configuring custom DNS servers on managed networks
Keep a fallback DNS configuration in mind for restricted networks
Document which networks intentionally restrict DNS choices

description: An outdated or incorrect DNS entry remains stored in the local DNS cache, causing a website or service to fail to load or resolve to the wrong address even after the actual DNS record has been corrected.
symptoms: A website resolves to an old, incorrect, or non-existent IP address
The problem persists even though the DNS record has been confirmed correct elsewhere
Other devices, or the same device using a different DNS cache, resolve the site correctly
possible_causes: Local DNS resolver cache holding an old entry from before a recent DNS record change
Browser-level DNS cache separate from the operating system's cache
Router's own DNS cache holding outdated information for connected devices
Cached negative result (a previous failed lookup) preventing a fresh attempt
diagnostic_questions: Was there a recent change to this specific domain's DNS records, such as moving to a new server?
How long ago was the DNS change made, and has enough time passed for normal propagation?
Have you tried a completely different device or network to see if the site resolves correctly there?
Have you tried flushing the DNS cache on both the operating system and the browser?

commands.purpose: Clear the Windows operating system's local DNS resolver cache
commands.expected_result: 'Successfully flushed the DNS Resolver Cache'
commands.abnormal_result: An error message, though this is uncommon; the command should generally succeed

commands.purpose: Perform a fresh lookup after flushing to see if a new, correct result is returned
commands.expected_result: Returns the correct, updated IP address
commands.abnormal_result: Still returns the old, incorrect address, suggesting the outdated entry is cached elsewhere, such as at the router or ISP level

troubleshooting_steps.action: Flush the local operating system DNS cache using ipconfig /flushdns
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Clears the most common source of a stale cached entry on this specific device

troubleshooting_steps.action: Clear the browser's own DNS cache or fully restart the browser
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many browsers maintain a separate internal DNS cache independent of the operating system

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the router if it also caches DNS results for connected devices
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Router-level caching can continue to serve an old result even after the OS and browser caches are cleared

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test resolution from a completely different network, such as mobile data, to check if the correct new record has propagated more broadly
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps distinguish between a local caching issue and normal, still-in-progress DNS propagation across the internet

troubleshooting_steps.action: Wait for the record's TTL (time to live) to naturally expire if propagation is still in progress elsewhere
troubleshooting_steps.reason: DNS changes take time to propagate globally, and forcing a local flush cannot speed up caches on other networks/ISPs

possible_solutions: Flush the local OS DNS cache
Clear the browser's DNS cache or restart the browser
Restart the router to clear its DNS cache
Wait for normal DNS propagation if the change is very recent
prevention: Set reasonable TTL values on DNS records before making changes, especially ahead of planned migrations
Flush caches proactively after known DNS record changes
Communicate DNS change timelines to affected users in advance

description: The device shows no default gateway configured at all, or Windows reports the gateway as unavailable, preventing any traffic from leaving the local network.
symptoms: ipconfig shows no default gateway listed, or 'Default Gateway Not Available' in network diagnostics
Local network devices may be reachable, but internet access fails completely
Windows Network Troubleshooter specifically flags this as the issue
possible_causes: DHCP server did not provide a gateway address
Static IP configuration is missing the gateway field
Router is powered off or has crashed, so it is not responding to identify itself as the gateway
Network adapter driver issue preventing proper gateway detection
diagnostic_questions: Is this device using DHCP (automatic) or a static IP configuration?
Is the router powered on and functioning normally for other devices?
Does ipconfig show a blank or missing gateway field?
Does releasing and renewing the IP address resolve the issue?

commands.purpose: Check whether a default gateway address is present in the configuration
commands.expected_result: A valid gateway address is listed, matching the router's IP
commands.abnormal_result: Gateway field is blank or missing entirely

commands.purpose: Request a fresh, complete configuration including the gateway
commands.expected_result: A complete configuration including a valid gateway is received
commands.abnormal_result: The gateway remains missing after renewal, pointing to a router or DHCP-side issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check ipconfig /all to confirm whether the gateway field is genuinely blank
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms this is truly a missing gateway issue rather than an unrelated internet problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: For DHCP-based devices, release and renew the IP address to request a complete configuration again
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Often resolves a one-time failure to receive the gateway value during the initial request

troubleshooting_steps.action: For statically configured devices, check and correct the manually entered gateway field
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An incomplete static configuration will never include a valid gateway on its own

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the router is powered on and responding, since it is typically also the source of the gateway address via DHCP
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A router that is off or crashed cannot provide gateway information to any device

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the router if it is on but not properly responding to DHCP requests, including the gateway field
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves a partial service failure where the router is up but not fully functioning

possible_solutions: Release and renew the IP address for DHCP clients
Manually correct the gateway field for static IP configurations
Restart the router if it is not properly providing gateway information
Update the network adapter driver if the problem persists on one device only
prevention: Ensure DHCP scope configuration always includes a valid gateway option
Document required static configuration values, including the gateway, for reference
Regularly verify router health and DHCP service functionality

description: The default gateway address is properly configured, but the device cannot actually reach or communicate with it, blocking all traffic beyond the local segment.
symptoms: ipconfig shows a valid gateway address, but pinging it fails
Local network devices on the same subnet may or may not be reachable depending on the exact cause
No internet or outside network access as a direct result
possible_causes: Router is powered off, crashed, or rebooting
Physical or wireless connection to the router is down or unstable
Device and gateway are actually on different, non-communicating network segments despite appearing configured correctly
Switch or cabling issue between the device and the router
diagnostic_questions: Can you ping the configured gateway address at all?
Is the router visibly powered on with normal status lights?
Are other devices on the same network able to reach the gateway successfully?
Is there any switch or additional networking equipment between this device and the router that could be at fault?

commands.purpose: Directly test connectivity to the configured gateway address
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Request timed out, confirming the gateway is unreachable despite being correctly configured

commands.purpose: Trace the path to the gateway to see how far traffic gets before failing
commands.expected_result: Reaches the gateway in a single hop
commands.abnormal_result: Fails immediately at the first hop, confirming a direct local connectivity problem to the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ping the configured gateway address to confirm it is indeed unreachable
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Verifies the problem precisely before investigating further

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if the router is powered on and showing normal status lights
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A router that is off or has crashed will obviously be unreachable as a gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the physical or wireless connection between the device and the router, including any intermediate switches
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A broken link anywhere along this path will prevent reaching the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test from another device on the same network to see if the gateway is reachable from there
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines if this is isolated to one device or affects the whole local segment

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the router and, if applicable, any intermediate switches
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves temporary crashes or hangs preventing the router from responding as expected

possible_solutions: Restart the router if it is unresponsive
Check and repair the physical or wireless connection to the router
Check and restart any intermediate switches between the device and router
Verify the correct gateway address is configured if reachability issues persist
prevention: Use quality, well-maintained cabling and switches between devices and the router
Keep router firmware updated for stability
Monitor router uptime and responsiveness on critical networks

description: Multiple devices across the network have an incorrect default gateway configuration, typically due to a router change or a DHCP server handing out the wrong value to everyone.
symptoms: Many or all devices on the network lose internet access at the same time
Devices show a gateway address that does not match the router's actual current IP
Problem started right after a router replacement, firmware update, or IP address change
possible_causes: Router's IP address was changed, but DHCP scope options were not updated to match
Router was replaced with a new device using a different default IP
DHCP server configuration manually set with an outdated or incorrect gateway value
Static IP devices across the network were configured with an old gateway value that is no longer correct
diagnostic_questions: Did the router get replaced, reset, or have its IP address changed recently?
Are multiple devices affected, or just one, which would suggest a device-specific rather than network-wide issue?
What gateway value are affected devices currently showing, and does it match the router's actual current IP?
Are the affected devices using DHCP, static IPs, or a mix of both?

commands.purpose: Confirm that multiple devices share the same incorrect gateway value
commands.expected_result: N/A - this simply confirms the scope of the issue across devices
commands.abnormal_result: Consistent incorrect gateway value across many devices strongly suggests a network-wide DHCP misconfiguration rather than isolated device issues

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the router's actual current IP address from its own administration interface or physical label
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes the correct value that all devices should be using as their gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the DHCP server's scope options for the gateway value being distributed to clients
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Identifies whether the DHCP server itself is the source of the incorrect network-wide configuration

troubleshooting_steps.action: Correct the DHCP scope's gateway option to match the router's actual current IP address
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ensures all future DHCP clients receive the correct value automatically

troubleshooting_steps.action: Have all affected DHCP-based devices release and renew their IP address to pick up the corrected gateway
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Existing devices will not automatically receive the fix until their next renewal

troubleshooting_steps.action: Manually correct the gateway on any statically configured devices, since these will not be fixed by the DHCP correction
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Static devices require individual manual updates since they do not use DHCP

possible_solutions: Correct the DHCP scope's gateway option to match the router's actual IP
Have DHCP clients release and renew to receive the corrected gateway
Manually update the gateway on any statically configured devices
Document the router's IP address clearly after any changes
prevention: Update DHCP scope options immediately whenever the router's IP address changes
Maintain a checklist for router replacement or reconfiguration procedures
Regularly audit static IP device configurations for accuracy
keywords: all devices lost internet after router change

description: Requests to the gateway or through it to reach external destinations take an unusually long time and eventually time out, rather than failing immediately or succeeding normally.
symptoms: Web browsers show a '504 Gateway Timeout' error or similar
Ping to the gateway itself may succeed, but requests passing through it to reach further destinations time out
Problem may be intermittent rather than constant
possible_causes: Router or gateway device is overloaded and slow to process traffic
Upstream connection (to the ISP) beyond the gateway is degraded or intermittent
Gateway device is experiencing a hardware or software issue causing slow processing
Excessive traffic or a misbehaving device on the network overwhelming the gateway
diagnostic_questions: Does the timeout happen consistently or only intermittently?
Is the gateway (router) itself reachable via ping, even if traffic through it times out?
Are there any devices on the network generating unusually high traffic, such as large downloads or a misbehaving application?
Does restarting the router temporarily resolve the timeouts?

commands.purpose: Check if the gateway itself responds consistently, even if traffic through it is slow
commands.expected_result: Consistent, timely replies from the gateway
commands.abnormal_result: Slow or inconsistent replies suggest the gateway device itself is under strain

commands.purpose: See where along the path beyond the gateway delays or failures begin
commands.expected_result: Reasonable response times at each hop
commands.abnormal_result: Significant delay or failure starting right at or just after the gateway hop

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ping the gateway repeatedly to check if it responds consistently and quickly on its own
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines if the gateway device itself is struggling versus the issue being further upstream

troubleshooting_steps.action: Run tracert to a public destination to see exactly where delays begin along the path
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps pinpoint whether the problem is at the gateway itself or beyond it toward the ISP

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for devices on the network consuming excessive bandwidth or generating heavy traffic
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An overloaded gateway from heavy local traffic can cause timeouts for other devices' requests

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the gateway/router device to clear any temporary processing overload or software issue
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Resolves many temporary performance problems causing timeouts

troubleshooting_steps.action: Contact the ISP if delays are confirmed to begin just beyond the gateway, indicating an upstream issue
troubleshooting_steps.reason: The problem may be outside the local network and require ISP-side investigation

possible_solutions: Restart the gateway/router device
Identify and manage devices consuming excessive bandwidth
Contact the ISP if upstream delays are confirmed beyond the gateway
Consider upgrading gateway hardware if it is consistently overloaded
prevention: Monitor gateway device performance and traffic load periodically
Keep gateway/router firmware updated
Set up bandwidth management or quality of service rules for critical traffic

description: Some packets sent to or through the gateway are lost, causing intermittent connectivity issues, choppy calls, or unreliable access to anything beyond the local network.
symptoms: Ping tests to the gateway show a percentage of lost packets rather than a complete failure
Intermittent connectivity issues affecting real-time applications like calls or games
Local network access to other devices may be unaffected, isolating the issue to the gateway specifically
possible_causes: Gateway device is overloaded and dropping packets under load
Faulty cable or port connecting the device to the gateway
WiFi interference if connected wirelessly to the gateway
Gateway hardware beginning to fail
diagnostic_questions: What percentage of packet loss are you seeing when pinging the gateway directly?
Is the connection to the gateway wired or wireless?
Does packet loss happen consistently or only during periods of heavy network use?
Have you tried a different cable or port when connecting to the gateway?

commands.purpose: Send many pings to the gateway to calculate an accurate packet loss percentage
commands.expected_result: 0% or very minimal packet loss
commands.abnormal_result: Noticeable packet loss percentage, confirming a real problem specifically with reaching the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Run an extended ping test directly to the gateway and note the packet loss percentage
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Quantifies the severity and confirms the problem is specifically between this device and the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: If wired, replace the cable and try a different port on the gateway device
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A damaged cable or failing port is a common physical cause of packet loss to the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: If wireless, check for interference and consider moving closer to the gateway or switching to a wired connection for testing
troubleshooting_steps.reason: WiFi issues are a very common source of loss specifically on the hop closest to the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if packet loss correlates with periods of heavy network usage by other devices
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An overloaded gateway may only drop packets under load, pointing to a capacity issue rather than a hardware fault

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the gateway device to rule out a temporary software issue, and consider hardware replacement if loss continues consistently
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Persistent packet loss even when idle and after a restart suggests a genuine hardware problem with the gateway

possible_solutions: Replace cables or try different ports on the gateway
Reduce WiFi interference or switch to a wired connection for testing
Restart the gateway device
Consider gateway hardware replacement if packet loss persists after other fixes
prevention: Use quality cables and connections to the gateway
Monitor gateway performance and packet loss trends over time
Avoid overloading gateway devices with excessive simultaneous traffic

description: Pinging the network's default gateway (usually the router) fails, which is a fundamental sign that the device cannot reach even the first step of its network path.
symptoms: ping <gateway_ip> returns 'Request timed out' or 'Destination host unreachable'
No internet or outside network access as a direct consequence
Local device-to-device communication may still work depending on the exact cause
possible_causes: Physical or wireless connection between the device and the router is down
Router is powered off or has crashed
Incorrect gateway address configured on the device
Firewall on the device blocking outbound ping (ICMP) traffic
diagnostic_questions: Is the physical cable connected, or is WiFi showing as connected?
Is the router powered on with normal status lights?
Is the gateway address configured on this device actually correct?
Have you tried pinging the gateway from another device on the same network?

commands.purpose: Directly test connectivity to the configured gateway
commands.expected_result: Replies received with reasonable response times
commands.abnormal_result: Request timed out, confirming the gateway cannot be reached

commands.purpose: Confirm the exact gateway address currently configured
commands.expected_result: A gateway address matching the router's actual IP
commands.abnormal_result: Missing or incorrect gateway address explains the ping failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the physical or wireless connection to the network is actually established
troubleshooting_steps.reason: No connection at all will naturally prevent reaching any destination, including the gateway

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the gateway address shown by ipconfig matches the router's actual current IP address
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An incorrect gateway address will always fail to respond, since it may not correspond to any real device

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check that the router is powered on and displaying normal status lights
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An offline or crashed router obviously cannot respond to any ping requests

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test pinging the gateway from a different device on the same network
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines whether the problem is isolated to this one device or affects the whole network

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the device's firewall settings for any rule blocking outbound ICMP (ping) traffic
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some firewalls block ping specifically while still allowing other types of traffic, which can be misleading

possible_solutions: Restart the router if it is unresponsive
Correct the gateway address if misconfigured
Check and repair the physical or wireless connection
Adjust firewall settings if blocking ICMP traffic
prevention: Regularly verify gateway configuration matches the router's actual address
Keep router firmware updated for reliability
Document firewall rules affecting ICMP traffic for troubleshooting reference

description: Pinging another device on the same local network fails, even though both devices appear to have valid IP addresses and are connected to the same network.
symptoms: ping <local_device_ip> returns 'Request timed out' or 'Destination host unreachable'
Both devices can typically reach the internet fine, isolating the issue to communication between them specifically
May affect only certain device pairs while others communicate normally
possible_causes: Devices are actually on different subnets or VLANs despite appearing to be on the same network
Firewall on the target device blocking incoming ping requests
Client isolation or AP isolation enabled on the router/access point
Target device is asleep, in low-power mode, or has its network adapter disabled
diagnostic_questions: Are both devices confirmed to be on the exact same subnet, based on their IP addresses and subnet masks?
Is the target device powered on and awake, not in sleep or hibernation?
Does the target device's firewall typically allow ping (ICMP) requests?
Is this a WiFi network with client/AP isolation potentially enabled?

commands.purpose: Compare IP addresses and subnet masks to confirm both devices are truly on the same logical network
commands.expected_result: Both devices share the same subnet based on their IP and mask
commands.abnormal_result: Devices are actually on different subnets despite being on the same physical WiFi/network, explaining the failure

commands.purpose: Test direct connectivity between the two local devices
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout confirms the two devices cannot communicate directly

troubleshooting_steps.action: Compare the IP address and subnet mask of both devices to confirm they are genuinely on the same logical subnet
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Devices that only appear to be on the same network but are actually on different subnets or VLANs cannot communicate directly without a router

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the target device is powered on and not in sleep or hibernation mode
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many devices stop responding to network requests, including ping, while asleep

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the target device's firewall settings to confirm it allows incoming ICMP (ping) requests
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many firewalls block ping by default even while allowing normal application traffic, which can be misleading during troubleshooting

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the router or access point for client isolation or AP isolation settings, which intentionally prevent connected devices from communicating with each other
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This is a common and often overlooked router security feature that blocks exactly this kind of local device-to-device communication

troubleshooting_steps.action: Disable client/AP isolation temporarily to test if that resolves the issue, then decide if it should stay off
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms this specific setting as the cause before making a permanent change

possible_solutions: Confirm both devices are on the same subnet
Wake the target device from sleep/hibernation
Adjust the target device's firewall to allow ICMP if appropriate
Disable client/AP isolation on the router if it is blocking local communication
prevention: Document router isolation settings and their intended purpose
Keep devices on the same subnet when local communication is required
Configure firewalls thoughtfully to allow necessary local traffic
keywords: devices cant see each other same network

description: Pinging a specific server, whether local or remote, fails, preventing basic connectivity testing and likely also blocking the actual service the server provides.
symptoms: ping <server_address> returns 'Request timed out' or similar failure
The service hosted on that server (website, application, file share) is also inaccessible
Other servers or destinations may still be reachable normally
possible_causes: Server itself is down or unreachable
Firewall on the server or along the network path blocking ICMP specifically while still allowing the actual service traffic
Incorrect server address or DNS resolution issue if using a hostname
Network routing issue between the client and the server's network
diagnostic_questions: Are you pinging the server by IP address or by hostname?
Is the actual service on the server (website, application) also failing, or does ping fail while the service still works?
Is this server on the local network or accessed remotely over the internet?
Have other users or devices reported the same issue reaching this server?

commands.purpose: Test basic reachability to the server
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout, though note that many servers intentionally block ICMP for security while the actual service still works fine

commands.purpose: Trace the network path to the server to identify where connectivity fails
commands.expected_result: Path completes to the server
commands.abnormal_result: Path stops at a specific hop, indicating where along the route the connection breaks

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm whether the actual service on the server (like a website or application) works despite ping failing
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many servers deliberately block ICMP ping for security reasons while their actual services function normally; this is not a real problem if the service itself works

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the actual service also fails, run tracert to see how far along the path traffic gets before failing
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Identifies whether the failure is local, at an intermediate network point, or right at the server itself

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the server address is correct, especially if using a hostname that depends on DNS resolution
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An incorrect address or failed DNS lookup would explain a failure that has nothing to do with the server's actual availability

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check with other users or from a different network to see if the server is reachable elsewhere
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps determine if the issue is specific to your network path or affects everyone trying to reach the server

troubleshooting_steps.action: Contact the server administrator or hosting provider if the server appears down or unreachable from multiple locations
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms and escalates a genuine server-side outage that is outside local control

possible_solutions: Confirm if the actual service works despite ping being blocked, which requires no fix
Verify the correct server address/hostname is being used
Test connectivity from a different network to isolate the problem's location
Contact the server administrator if the server is confirmed down
prevention: Understand that ping being blocked does not always indicate a real problem
Keep server addresses and access documentation up to date
Test critical server connectivity from multiple network locations periodically

description: Pinging any destination beyond the local network, such as a public IP address or website, consistently fails, even though local devices may be reachable normally.
symptoms: ping 8.8.8.8 or any public address returns 'Request timed out'
Local network devices, including the gateway, may still be pingable
No internet access as a direct result across possibly all applications
possible_causes: Router has no internet connection from the ISP (WAN down)
DNS issue if pinging by hostname rather than a raw IP address
Firewall blocking outbound internet traffic specifically
ISP outage affecting the connection beyond the local network
diagnostic_questions: Can you successfully ping the local gateway/router, even though pinging the internet fails?
Are you pinging by IP address (like 8.8.8.8) or by a hostname (like google.com)?
Does the router's WAN/internet status light look normal?
Do other devices on the same network also fail to reach the internet?

commands.purpose: Confirm whether the local network segment works before testing further out
commands.expected_result: Replies received from the gateway
commands.abnormal_result: If this also fails, the problem is local connectivity, not specifically an internet/WAN issue

commands.purpose: Test connectivity to a known public IP address beyond the local network
commands.expected_result: Replies received
commands.abnormal_result: Timeout while the gateway ping succeeds confirms the router has no working internet connection

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ping the local gateway first to confirm the local network segment itself is working
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes whether the problem is purely about reaching beyond the local network or a broader local issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Ping a known public IP address like 8.8.8.8 directly, bypassing DNS, to test raw internet reachability
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether this is a pure connectivity problem versus a DNS-specific issue if a hostname was used instead

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the router's WAN/internet status light and admin interface for a connected status
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the router itself has lost its connection to the ISP

troubleshooting_steps.action: Restart the modem and router to resolve temporary WAN connectivity issues
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Addresses the majority of common causes for a router losing its internet connection

troubleshooting_steps.action: Contact the ISP if the WAN remains down after a restart and the outage is confirmed to be beyond the local network
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Indicates a genuine outage or line problem outside local control

possible_solutions: Restart the modem and router to restore the WAN connection
Verify the issue is not DNS-related by testing with a raw IP address
Contact the ISP if the outage is confirmed on their end
prevention: Monitor router WAN status periodically
Keep modem and router firmware updated
Use a UPS to protect against power-related WAN drops

description: A ping attempt to any destination results in the specific message 'Request timed out', indicating the request was sent but no response was received within the expected time.
symptoms: Output specifically shows 'Request timed out' rather than an immediate error
May happen for some pings in a sequence while others succeed, or consistently for all
Applies to local devices, the gateway, or internet destinations depending on the situation
possible_causes: Target device or destination is unreachable, offline, or not responding
Firewall on the target or along the path silently dropping ICMP requests
Network congestion causing the response to arrive too late or be lost
Incorrect IP address or destination being pinged
diagnostic_questions: Is the timeout happening for all destinations you try to ping, or just specific ones?
Is the target device or server confirmed to be powered on and connected?
Does this happen consistently, or only intermittently for the same destination?
Have you double-checked the IP address or hostname being pinged for accuracy?

commands.purpose: Send multiple ping attempts to see if timeouts happen consistently or only some of the time
commands.expected_result: Consistent replies with no timeouts
commands.abnormal_result: A pattern of some or all requests timing out, helping to characterize the severity of the problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the exact IP address or hostname being pinged is correct
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A simple typo or wrong address will naturally result in every request timing out

troubleshooting_steps.action: Send several ping attempts in a row to see if timeouts happen consistently or only intermittently
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Consistent timeouts suggest the destination is truly unreachable, while intermittent ones suggest congestion or instability

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check if the specific target's firewall may be blocking or dropping ICMP echo requests silently
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This is extremely common and does not necessarily indicate the target device or service is actually broken

troubleshooting_steps.action: Try pinging a different, known-reliable destination to compare results
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps determine if the timeout issue is specific to this one destination or reflects a broader network problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Investigate network path and equipment (cables, router, switch) if timeouts happen for multiple different destinations
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Points toward a local network issue rather than a problem with any single specific destination

possible_solutions: Confirm the correct destination address is being used
Determine if ICMP is simply being blocked, which may not indicate a real problem
Investigate local network equipment if timeouts affect multiple destinations
Test alternate destinations to isolate the scope of the issue
prevention: Understand that timeouts to specific destinations may be normal due to firewall policy
